The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary abused AWS Systems Manager Inventory to identify targets on the compromised network prior to lateral movement. (4) the adversary has used servers under their control to validate tracking pixels sent to phishing victims. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has detached network shares after exfiltrating files, likely to evade detection. (2) the adversary has staged tools, including gsecdump and WCE, on previously compromised websites. (3) the adversary has used RAR to compress, encrypt, and password-protect files prior to exfiltration. (4) the adversary actors use at to schedule tasks to run self-extracting RAR archives, which install HTTPBrowser or PlugX on other victims on a network. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has been observed making videos of victims to observe bank employees day to day activities. (2) the adversary has used RAdmin, a remote software tool used to remotely control workstations and ATMs. (3) the adversary has injected a DLL library containing a Trojan into the fwmain32.exe process. (4) the adversary has used port 444 when sending data about the system from the client to the server. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has compromised domains for use in targeted malicious campaigns. (2) the adversary has set up websites with malicious hyperlinks and iframes to infect targeted victims with Crimson, njRAT, and other malicious tools. (4) the adversary has used websites with malicious hyperlinks and iframes to infect targeted victims with Crimson, njRAT, and other malicious tools. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has abused the Outlook Home Page feature for persistence. the adversary has also used CVE-2017-11774 to roll back the initial patch designed to protect against Home Page abuse. (2) the adversary has used DNS for C2 including the publicly available requestbin.net tunneling service. (3) the adversary has used credential dumping tool named VALUEVAULT to steal credentials from the Windows Credential Manager. (4) the adversary has leveraged compromised organizations to conduct supply chain attacks on government entities. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has created self-signed certificates from fictitious and spoofed legitimate software companies that were later used to sign malware. (2) the adversary apparently altered NDiskMonitor samples by adding four bytes of random letters in a likely attempt to change the file hashes. (3) the adversary apparently altered NDiskMonitor samples by adding four bytes of random letters in a likely attempt to change the file hashes. (4) the adversary hides base64-encoded and encrypted C2 server locations in comments on legitimate websites. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has used icons mimicking MS Office files to mask malicious executables. the adversary has also attempted to hide executables by changing the file extension to ".scr" to mimic Windows screensavers. (2) the adversary has used compromised websites to register custom URL schemes on a remote system. (3) the adversary has used malware to identify installed AV and commonly used forensic and malware analysis tools. (4) the adversary has sent spearphishing emails with links to harvest credentials and deliver malware. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has used Group Policy to deploy batch scripts for ransomware deployment. (2) the adversary has used a customized version of the Impacket wmiexec.py module to create renamed output files. (3) the adversary has used the Iox and NPS proxy and tunneling tools in combination create multiple connections through a single tunnel. (4) the adversary has used a customized version of the Iox port-forwarding and proxy tool. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has used pcalua.exe to obfuscate binary execution and remote connections. (2) the adversary has used cloud storage to exfiltrate data, in particular the megatools utilities were used to exfiltrate data to Mega, a file storage service. (3) the adversary has used a Python script to establish outbound communication and to execute commands using SMB port 445. (4) the adversary has used malware with string encryption. the adversary has also encrypted data and has encoded PowerShell commands using Base64. the adversary has used `PyArmor` to obfuscate code execution of LaZagne. Additionally, the adversary has obfuscated downloaded files by renaming them as commonly used tools and has used `echo`, instead of file names themselves, to execute files. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has collected lists of names for individuals from targeted organizations. (2) the adversary has cloned victim organization login pages and staged them for later use in credential harvesting campaigns. the adversary has also made use of a variety of URL shorteners for these staged websites. (3) the adversary has set up auto forwarding rules on compromised e-mail accounts. (4) the adversary has searched victim's websites to identify the interests and academic areas of targeted individuals and to scrape source code, branding, and organizational contact information for phishing pages. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has used batch scripts that can disable the Windows firewall on specific remote machines. (2) the adversary has built malware, such as DCSrv and PyDCrypt, for targeting victims' machines. (3) the adversary has used signed drivers from an open source tool called DiskCryptor to evade detection. (4) the adversary has exploited known vulnerabilities in public-facing infrastructure such as Microsoft Exchange Servers. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has used CMSTP.exe and a malicious INF to execute its POWERSTATS payload. (2) the adversary has sent phishing emails to targets from the email address support@microsoftonlines[.]com. (4) the adversary has leveraged ClickFix type tactics enticing victims to copy and paste malicious PowerShell code. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has created forged Kerberos Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) and Ticket Granting Service (TGS) tickets to maintain administrative access. (2) the adversary has placed malware on file shares and given it the same name as legitimate documents on the share. (3) the adversary has used at to register a scheduled task to execute malware during lateral movement. (4) the adversary has used RC4 encryption (for Datper malware) and AES (for xxmm malware) to obfuscate HTTP traffic. the adversary has also used a tool called RarStar that encodes data with a custom XOR algorithm when posting it to a C2 server. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has used the Office Test persistence mechanism within Microsoft Office by adding the Registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Office test\Special\Perf to execute code. (2) the adversary has used a Wi-Fi Pineapple to set up Evil Twin Wi-Fi Poisoning for the purposes of capturing victim credentials or planting espionage-oriented malware. (3) the adversary uses a tool that captures information from air-gapped computers via an infected USB and transfers it to network-connected computer when the USB is inserted. (4) the adversary added "junk data" to each encoded string, preventing trivial decoding without knowledge of the junk removal algorithm. Each implant was given a "junk length" value when created, tracked by the controller software to allow seamless communication but prevent analysis of the command protocol on the wire. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has leveraged LLMs to search for official emails to build target lists, and conduct reconnaissance on potential business partners. (2) the adversary has deleted login notification emails and has cleared the Sent folder to cover their tracks. (3) the adversary has intercepted SMS-based one-time passwords and has set up two-factor authentication. Additionally, the adversary has used cloned or fake websites to capture MFA tokens. (4) the adversary has used tools such as NICECURL with command and control communication taking place over HTTPS. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has used the the PuTTY suite Secure Copy Protocol (SCP) client for file transfer. (2) the adversary has used a tool named MRSAStealer as a password filter to collect credentials on password changes. (3) the adversary has crafted malware payloads to appear as Privacy-Enhanced Mail (PEM) files. (4) the adversary has deployed shellcode to check for Japanese Microsoft Office settings. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary uses the built-in Nltest utility or tools such as AdFind to enumerate Active Directory trusts in victim environments. (2) the adversary has accessed and downloaded information stored in SharePoint instances as part of data gathering and exfiltration activity. (3) the adversary uses legitimate utilities such as AnyDesk and PuTTy for maintaining remote access to victim environments. (4) the adversary engages in double-extortion ransomware, exfiltrating files then encrypting them, in order to prompt victims to pay a ransom. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary packed some payloads using different types of packers, both known and custom. (2) the adversary used reg commands to dump specific hives from the Windows Registry, such as the SAM hive, and obtain password hashes. (3) the adversary ensured each payload had a unique hash, including by using different types of packers. (4) the adversary used a modified version of HTRAN in which they obfuscated strings such as debug messages in an apparent attempt to evade detection. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has abused email forwarding rules to monitor the activities of a victim, steal information, and maintain persistent access after compromised credentials are reset. (2) the adversary has sent emails to establish rapport with targets eventually sending messages with attachments containing links to credential-stealing sites. (3) the adversary has used open-source research to identify information about victims to use in targeting. (4) the adversary has used EvilGinx to steal the session cookies of victims directed to phishing domains. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has used the Windows Script Host (wscript) to execute intermediate files written to victim machines. (2) the adversary clones .NET assemblies from other .NET binaries as well as cloning code signing certificates from other software to obfuscate the initial loader payload. (3) the adversary has delivered malicious Microsoft Office files containing an embedded JavaScript object that would, on execution, download and execute OutSteel and the adversary Bot. (4) the adversary gathered victim email information in advance of phishing operations for targeted attacks. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary modified the ld.so preload file in Linux environments to enable persistence for Winnti malware. (2) the adversary used the last command in Linux environments to identify recently logged-in users on victim machines. (3) the adversary enumerated logs related to authentication in Linux environments prior to deleting selective entries for defense evasion purposes. (4) the adversary used remote scheduled tasks to install malicious software on victim systems during lateral movement actions. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has used obfuscated VBScripts with randomly generated variable names and concatenated strings. (2) A the adversary file stealer has the capability to steal data from newly connected logical volumes on a system, including USB drives. (3) the adversary has inserted malicious macros into existing documents, providing persistence when they are reopened. the adversary has loaded the the adversary's previously delivered VBA project by relaunching Microsoft Outlook with the /altvba option, once the Application.Startup event is received. (4) the adversary has used fast flux DNS to mask their command and control channel behind rotating IP addresses. Additionally, the adversary has used a low-frequency variant of the single-flux method. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary used a renamed version of rundll32.exe, such as "dbengin.exe" located in the `ProgramData\Microsoft\PlayReady` directory, to proxy malicious DLL execution. (2) the adversary used Reg to dump the Security Account Manager (SAM) hive from victim machines for follow-on credential extraction. (3) the adversary compromised web servers hosting updates for software as part of a supply chain intrusion. (4) the adversary is associated with several supply chain compromises using malicious updates to compromise victims. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has created and used new accounts within a victim's Active Directory environment to maintain persistence. (2) the adversary has utilized the PowerShell script `Get-DataInfo.ps1` to collect installed backup software information from a compromised machine. (3) the adversary has used batch scripts that utilizes WMIC to execute a BITSAdmin transfer of a ransomware payload to each compromised machine. (4) the adversary has used Rubeus, MimiKatz Kerberos module, and the Invoke-Kerberoast cmdlet to steal AES hashes. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has queried the Kubernetes API for local service account tokens and has used `kubectl` for lateral movement. (2) the adversary has modified software packages with preinstall scripts to download and execute malicious payloads. (3) the adversary has compromised trusted CI/CD pipelines by injecting credential-stealing payloads into legitimate workflows and software packages including open-source security tools Trivy and KICS, and AI gateway LiteLLM. (4) the adversary has conducted coordinated supply chain attacks targeting open-source developer infrastructure including the NPM, VS Code, Docker, and PyPi ecosystems to compromise multiple software packages. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary actors used the following command following exploitation of a machine with LOWBALL malware to obtain information about services: net start >> %temp%\download (2) the adversary actors used the following command following exploitation of a machine with LOWBALL malware to list local groups: net localgroup administrator >> %temp%\download (3) the adversary actors used the following commands following exploitation of a machine with LOWBALL malware to enumerate user accounts: net user >> %temp%\download net user /domain >> %temp%\download (4) the adversary actors used the following command following exploitation of a machine with LOWBALL malware to display network connections: netstat -ano >> %temp%\download Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has sent e-mails with malicious attachments that lead victims to credential harvesting websites. (2) the adversary has configured tools to automatically send collected files to attacker controlled servers. (3) the adversary has used the ActiveXObject utility to create OLE objects to obtain execution through Internet Explorer. (4) the adversary has sent e-mails with malicious links to credential harvesting websites. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has compromised domains for some of their infrastructure, including for C2 and staging malware. (2) the adversary has crafted generic lures for spam campaigns to collect emails and credentials for targeting efforts. (3) the adversary has sent Microsoft Office Publisher documents to victims that have embedded malicious macros that execute an hta file via calling `mshta.exe`. (4) the adversary uses a loader DLL file to collect AV product names from an infected host. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary typically uses commercial VPN services for anonymizing last-hop traffic to victim networks, such as ProtonVPN. (2) the adversary engaged in various brute forcing activities via SMB in victim environments. (3) the adversary exfiltrated staged data using tools such as Putty and WinSCP, communicating with command and control servers. (4) the adversary tunnels RDP traffic through deployed web shells to access victim environments via compromised accounts. the adversary used the Plink tool to tunnel RDP connections for remote access and lateral movement in victim environments. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has used TLS encrypted C2 communications including for campaigns using AsyncRAT. (2) the adversary has injected malicious code into legitimate .NET related processes including regsvcs.exe, msbuild.exe, and installutil.exe. (3) the adversary has used multiple strains of malware available for purchase on criminal forums or in open-source repositories. (4) the adversary has used VBS files to execute or establish persistence for additional payloads, often using file names consistent with email themes or mimicking system functionality. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has used Process Doppelgänging to evade security software while deploying tools on compromised systems. (2) the adversary used several tools for retrieving login and password information, including LaZagne. (3) the adversary used several tools for retrieving login and password information, including LaZagne. (4) the adversary used a tool called Total SMB BruteForcer to perform internal password spraying. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has used wmic.exe and Windows Registry modifications to set the COR_PROFILER environment variable to execute a malicious DLL whenever a process loads the .NET CLR. (2) the adversary has used JuicyPotato to abuse the SeImpersonate token privilege to escalate from web application pool accounts to NT Authority\SYSTEM. (3) the adversary has executed custom-compiled XMRIG miner DLLs using regsvr32.exe. (4) the adversary has used mofcomp.exe to establish WMI Event Subscription persistence mechanisms configured from a *.mof file. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has rapidly transformed and adapted public exploit proof-of-concept code for new vulnerabilities and utilized them against target networks. (2) the adversary has compromised social media accounts to conduct social engineering attacks. (3) the adversary has received C2 instructions from user profiles created on legitimate websites such as Github and TechNet. (4) the adversary has used JavaScript to create a shortcut file in the Startup folder that points to its main backdoor. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has used a file stealer that can examine system drives, including those other than the C drive. (2) the adversary has used a weaponized Microsoft Word document with an embedded RTF exploit. (3) the adversary has used a file stealer to steal documents and images with the following extensions: txt, pdf, png, jpg, doc, xls, xlm, odp, ods, odt, rtf, ppt, xlsx, xlsm, docx, pptx, and jpeg. (4) the adversary has created scheduled tasks to maintain persistence on a compromised host. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has installed TightVNC server and client on compromised servers and endpoints for lateral movement. (2) the adversary has accessed victim security and IT environments and Microsoft Teams to mine valuable information. (3) the adversary has used Google Chrome bookmarks to identify internal resources and assets. (4) the adversary has exploited known vulnerabilities in remote services including RDP. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has used malicious USBs to emulate keystrokes to launch PowerShell to download and execute malware from the adversary's server. (2) the adversary has used Kerberoasting PowerShell commands such as, `Invoke-Kerberoast` for credential access and to enable lateral movement. (3) the adversary used images embedded into document lures that only activate the payload when a user double clicks to avoid sandboxes. (4) the adversary has created a fake link that redirected to an adversary-controlled Dropbox that downloaded the malicious executable. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has used phishing pages appearing like legitimate banking login portals to compromise credentials. (2) the adversary has used DDNS services such as DuckDNS, noip[.]com, and con-ip[.]com to redirect victims to sites or repositories hosting malware implants. (3) the adversary has used compromised Google Drive accounts including one associated with a Colombian government organization. (4) the adversary has used a botnet management interface to control large numbers of compromised hosts. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has avoided interacting with specific directories in order to reduce the likelihood of detection. (2) the adversary has utilized credential stuffing attacks to obtain initial access to victim environments. (3) the adversary has staged compressed files in specified locations prior to exfiltration over C2. (4) the adversary has abused built-in remote wipe or factory reset commands to wipe devices managed within an organization’s Cloud management solution impacting laptops, servers, and mobile devices. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has used PowerShell profiles to maintain persistence on an infected machine. (2) the adversary surveys a system upon check-in to discover Group Policy details using the gpresult command. (3) the adversary RPC backdoors can impersonate or steal process tokens before executing commands. (4) the adversary has modified variables in kernel memory to turn off Driver Signature Enforcement after exploiting vulnerabilities that obtained kernel mode privileges. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has collected location information from visitors to their phishing sites. (2) the adversary has collected names and passwords of all Wi-Fi networks to which a device has previously connected. (3) the adversary has created local accounts named `help` and `DefaultAccount` on compromised machines. (4) the adversary has captured the user-agent strings from visitors to their phishing sites. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has utilized an ORB (operational relay box) network – consisting compromised devices such as small office and home office (SOHO) routers, IoT devices, and leased virtual private servers (VPS) – to obfuscate the origin of C2 traffic. (2) the adversary has used the msiexec.exe command-line utility to download and execute malicious MSI files. (3) the adversary targeted presidential campaign staffers with credential phishing e-mails. (4) the adversary has compromised network devices such as small office and home office (SOHO) routers and IoT devices for ORB (operational relay box) Proxy networks. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has used vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs) to install malware and establish persistence across ESXi hypervisors. (2) the adversary used `vmtoolsd.exe` to run commands on guest virtual machines from a compromised ESXi host. (3) the adversary has used vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs) that contained modified descriptor XML files with the `acceptance-level` set to `partner` which allowed for privilege escalation. (4) the adversary has cleared specific events that contained the threat actor’s IP address from multiple log sources. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has used EarthWorm for network tunneling with a SOCKS5 server and port transfer functionalities. (2) the adversary has dropped legitimate software onto a compromised host and used it to execute malicious DLLs. (3) the adversary has used an executable to detect removable media, such as USB flash drives. (4) the adversary has obtained and used leaked malware, including DoublePulsar, EternalBlue, EternalRocks, and EternalSynergy, in its operations. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has used Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3) Browser and WinSCP to access S3 objects. (2) the adversary has executed API calls to enumerate permissions for compromised AWS accounts. (3) the adversary has compromised CI/CD pipelines by gaining access to high privilege engineering accounts on Git version control, BrowserStack, JFrog and other cloud project management platforms. (4) the adversary has searched through target companies’ GitHub repositories for login credentials or API keys. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has encrypted payloads using the Data Protection API (DPAPI), which relies on keys tied to specific user accounts on specific machines. the adversary has also environmentally keyed second stage malware with an RC5 key derived in part from the infected system's volume serial number. (2) the adversary uses the Chinese website fofa.su, similar to the Shodan scanning service, for passive scanning of victims. (3) the adversary leverages various tools and frameworks to brute-force directories on web servers. (4) the adversary transfers post-exploitation files dividing the payload into fixed-size chunks to evade detection. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary's malware has altered the NTLM authentication program on domain controllers to allow the adversary to login without a valid credential. (2) the adversary has used credential stuffing against victim's remote services to obtain valid accounts. (4) the adversary has used the NtdsAudit utility to collect information related to accounts and passwords. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has overwritten Linux system logs and unsets the Bash history file (effectively removing logging) during intrusions. (2) the adversary captured legitimate SSL certificates from victim organizations and installed these on the adversary-controlled infrastructure to enable subsequent adversary-in-the-middle operations. (3) the adversary modified DNS records at service providers to redirect traffic from legitimate resources to the adversary-controlled servers to enable adversary-in-the-middle attacks for credential capture. (4) the adversary modified Name Server (NS) items to refer to the adversary-controlled DNS servers to provide responses for all DNS lookups. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has used Cobalt Strike to empty log files. Additionally, the adversary has cleared all event logs using `wevutil`. (2) the adversary has used the win32_service WMI class to retrieve a list of services from the system. (3) the adversary has purchased access to victim VPNs to facilitate access to victim environments. (4) the adversary has served fake updates via legitimate websites that have been compromised. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary malware can download a remote access tool, ShiftyBug, and inject into another process. (2) the adversary malware can create a .lnk file and add a Registry Run key to establish persistence. (3) the adversary malware can use process hollowing to inject one of its trojans into another process. (4) the adversary has used -W Hidden to conceal PowerShell windows by setting the WindowStyle parameter to hidden. Which MITRE ATT&CK threat group (G-ID) is most consistent with this activity?

The following behaviours were observed in a single intrusion campaign: (1) the adversary has obtained credentials insecurely stored on targeted network appliances. In particular, accesses were permitted above state->allocated_stack, but not below it. In other words, if the stack was already "large enough", the access was permitted, but otherwise the access was rejected instead of being allowed to "grow the stack". This undesired rejection was happening in two places: - in check_stack_slot_within_bounds() - in check_stack_range_initialized() This patch arranges for these accesses to be permitted. A bunch of tests that were relying on the old rejection had to change; all of them were changed to add also run unprivileged, in which case the old behavior persists. One tests couldn't be updated - global_func16 - because it can't run unprivileged for other reasons.  This patch also fixes the tracking of the stack size for variable-offset reads. This second fix is bundled in the same commit as the first one because they're inter-related. Before this patch, writes to the stack using registers containing a variable offset (as opposed to registers with fixed, known values) were not properly contributing to the function's needed stack size. As a result, it was possible for a program to verify, but then to attempt to read out-of-bounds data at runtime because a too small stack had been allocated for it.  Each function tracks the size of the stack it needs in bpf_subprog_info.stack_depth, which is maintained by update_stack_depth(). For regular memory accesses, check_mem_access() was calling update_state_depth() but it was passing in only the fixed part of the offset register, ignoring the variable offset. This was incorrect; the minimum possible value of that register should be used instead.  This tracking is now fixed by centralizing the tracking of stack size in grow_stack_state(), and by lifting the calls to grow_stack_state() to check_stack_access_within_bounds() as suggested by Andrii. A vulnerability report states: "In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:  sctp: use call_rcu to free endpoint  This patch is to delay the endpoint free by calling call_rcu() to fix another use-after-free issue in sctp_sock_dump():    BUG: KASAN: use-after-free in __lock_acquire+0x36d9/0x4c20   Call Trace:     __lock_acquire+0x36d9/0x4c20 kernel/locking/lockdep.c:3218     lock_acquire+0x1ed/0x520 kernel/locking/lockdep.c:3844     __raw_spin_lock_bh include/linux/spinlock_api_smp.h:135 [inline]     _raw_spin_lock_bh+0x31/0x40 kernel/locking/spinlock.c:168     spin_lock_bh include/linux/spinlock.h:334 [inline]     __lock_sock+0x203/0x350 net/core/sock.c:2253     lock_sock_nested+0xfe/0x120 net/core/sock.c:2774     lock_sock include/net/sock.h:1492 [inline]     sctp_sock_dump+0x122/0xb20 net/sctp/diag.c:324     sctp_for_each_transport+0x2b5/0x370 net/sctp/socket.c:5091     sctp_diag_dump+0x3ac/0x660 net/sctp/diag.c:527     __inet_diag_dump+0xa8/0x140 net/ipv4/inet_diag.c:1049     inet_diag_dump+0x9b/0x110 net/ipv4/inet_diag.c:1065     netlink_dump+0x606/0x1080 net/netlink/af_netlink.c:2244     __netlink_dump_start+0x59a/0x7c0 net/netlink/af_netlink.c:2352     netlink_dump_start include/linux/netlink.h:216 [inline]     inet_diag_handler_cmd+0x2ce/0x3f0 net/ipv4/inet_diag.c:1170     __sock_diag_cmd net/core/sock_diag.c:232 [inline]     sock_diag_rcv_msg+0x31d/0x410 net/core/sock_diag.c:263     netlink_rcv_skb+0x172/0x440 net/netlink/af_netlink.c:2477     sock_diag_rcv+0x2a/0x40 net/core/sock_diag.c:274  This issue occurs when asoc is peeled off and the old sk is freed after getting it by asoc->base.sk and before calling lock_sock(sk).  To prevent the sk free, as a holder of the sk, ep should be alive when calling lock_sock(). This patch uses call_rcu() and moves sock_put and ep free into sctp_endpoint_destroy_rcu(), so that it's safe to try to hold the ep under rcu_read_lock in sctp_transport_traverse_process().  If sctp_endpoint_hold() returns true, it means this ep is still alive and we have held it and can continue to dump it; If it returns false, it means this ep is dead and can be freed after rcu_read_unlock, and we should skip it.  In sctp_sock_dump(), after locking the sk, if this ep is different from tsp->asoc->ep, it means during this dumping, this asoc was peeled off before calling lock_sock(), and the sk should be skipped; If this ep is the same with tsp->asoc->ep, it means no peeloff happens on this asoc, and due to lock_sock, no peeloff will happen either until release_sock.  Note that delaying endpoint free won't delay the port release, as the port release happens in sctp_endpoint_destroy() before calling call_rcu(). Also, freeing endpoint by call_rcu() makes it safe to access the sk by asoc->base.sk in sctp_assocs_seq_show() and sctp_rcv().
